summary: Describes an optional IPv6 Router Advertisement extension for sending default router preferences and more-specific routes to hosts. It helps multi-homed hosts pick an appropriate router when routers are on different links. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: If a house has two exits, one for the highway and one for the park, a sign tells you which door to use. This memo lets routers tell computers which exit is best for where they are going.

questions: what is the route information option
what is a type c host in ipv6
subtitle: How IPv6 routers can tell hosts which default router to prefer and which routes go where.

tldr.problem: A host with several routers, especially a multi-homed one with routers on different links, can pick the wrong one for a destination. Redirect messages only work within a single link.
tldr.mechanism: Router Advertisements gain a 2-bit default router preference and a new Route Information Option (type 24) that lists prefixes reachable through the router, each with its own preference and lifetime.
tldr.outcome: Hosts that understand the extension can choose routers sensibly, and hosts that do not keep working as before. Preferences and routes must be configured by an administrator, not derived from routing tables.

today: RFC 4191 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text calls the extension optional and backwards-compatible.

sections.title: Choosing Among Several Routers
sections.content:
In RFC 2461 Neighbor Discovery, a host keeps a Default Router List and a Prefix List, filled in from Router Advertisements. It uses the Prefix List to decide whether a destination is on-link and the Default Router List to pick a router for off-link destinations. When the list holds several routers, the choice matters: one router may perform much better than another, and the wrong one may mean no communication at all.

Redirect messages can correct a host's choice, but only within a single link. A router on one link cannot redirect a host to a router on another link, so Redirects do not help multi-homed hosts, such as a host with Ethernet plus wireless or a tunnel into a corporate network.

RFC 4191 defines an optional extension to Router Advertisements to fix this. It is backwards-compatible, so hosts that do not implement it work as well as before. The authors chose Router Advertisements over a protocol like RIP because they are an existing, stable router-to-host mechanism, piggybacking adds little overhead, and RIP does not carry route lifetimes.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a computer has two routers to choose from and picks the wrong one, like walking to the wrong door. This memo lets routers say which door is better.

sections.title: Preferences in the Router Advertisement
sections.content:
Preferences are encoded as a two-bit signed integer: 01 is High, 00 is Medium (the default), 11 is Low, and 10 is Reserved and MUST NOT be sent. With only three values the preference is clearly not a routing metric.

The Router Advertisement header gets a 2-bit Prf field after the M, O and H flags, and the rest of that byte is a 3-bit reserved field. If the Router Lifetime is zero, the sender MUST set the preference to 00 and the receiver MUST ignore it. A receiver that sees the Reserved value 10 MUST treat it as 00.

A Router Advertisement can also carry a Route Information Option for ::/0 with its own preference and lifetime. The RFC explains that the header preference is useful because it separates the best router for the default route from the router least likely to redirect common traffic, and it is more efficient than a separate option when both are the same router.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router can wear a badge that says High, Medium or Low. Medium means no special feeling either way.

sections.title: The Route Information Option
sections.content:
The Route Information Option uses option type 24. It tells hosts that a prefix is reachable through the advertising router. Its fields are the Length (in units of 8 octets), the Prefix Length (0 to 128), a 2-bit Route Preference, a 32-bit Route Lifetime in seconds, and the Prefix itself, which is 0, 8 or 16 octets long.

Length is 1, 2 or 3 depending on the Prefix Length: it must be 3 if the prefix length is greater than 64, and 2 or 3 if it is greater than 0. A Route Lifetime of all one bits (0xffffffff) means infinity. If a host receives the Reserved preference value in this option, it MUST ignore the whole option. A router MUST NOT put two options with the same prefix and prefix length in one Router Advertisement.

The authors used a new option rather than overloading the Prefix Information Option because prefixes usually appear in only one of them, the new option is typically 16 octets against 32, and it may be more compatible with some host implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a signpost that says 'to reach this neighbourhood, come through me', plus how long the sign is good for.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Host
sections.content:
The RFC describes three conceptual host models. Type A hosts ignore preferences and more-specific routes and behave exactly as in RFC 2461. Type B hosts add preference values to their Default Router List but ignore all Route Information Options. Type C hosts use a Routing Table in place of the Default Router List, with a prefix, prefix length, preference, lifetime and next-hop router for each entry, and they use both the header preference and the options.

A type C host first updates its ::/0 route from the Router Lifetime and header preference, then processes each Route Information Option. A ::/0 option overrides the header values. A route with lifetime zero is removed, and a route with a non-zero lifetime is added or refreshed. Whenever the table changes, the host MUST invalidate or remove affected Destination Cache entries.

For example, a router X advertises a lifetime of 100 seconds and Medium preference in its header, plus a ::/0 option with a lifetime of 200 seconds and Low preference. A type A host stores router X for 100 seconds. A type B host stores it as Medium for 100 seconds. A type C host stores ::/0 via X as Low for 200 seconds.

Type B and C hosts MAY allow local configuration of preferences that override those received, which helps with routers that do not support preferences.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers ignore the signs, some read only the badge, and some read the badge and every signpost. The more they read, the better they choose.

sections.title: How a Host Picks the Next Hop
sections.content:
A type B host consults its Default Router List and primarily prefers reachable routers over unreachable ones, then uses the preference values. A type C host searches its Routing Table for the route with the longest matching prefix, using preference as a tie-breaker between routes with the same prefix length. If the best route points to an unreachable router, it remembers that router and tries the next best, repeating until it finds a reachable router or runs out of routes. If no route matches at all, a type C host SHOULD discard the packet and report Destination Unreachable/No Route To Destination to the upper layer. A host with no reachability information assumes the router is reachable.

When a host skips an unreachable router X and sends to a router Y instead, it SHOULD probe X with a single Neighbor Solicitation, but only when it has useful traffic that it would have sent to X. Probes MUST be rate-limited to no more than one per minute per router. This lets the host return to X soon after it recovers, instead of waiting for X's next advertisement, which could take up to 30 minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer looks for the most specific road sign first. If two signs are equally specific it takes the one marked best, and if that road is closed it tries the next one and checks now and then whether the first has reopened.

sections.title: Router Configuration and Examples
sections.content:
Routers SHOULD NOT advertise preferences or routes by default, and SHOULD NOT dump their whole routing table to hosts. Routers SHOULD NOT send more than 17 Route Information Options per link, an arbitrary bound meant to keep the advertised routes few and carefully chosen. Preference values SHOULD be configured, not derived from routing metrics, and unstable routes SHOULD NOT be announced to hosts until they settle. When a router stops advertising, it SHOULD set the Route Lifetime to zero in all options as well.

For administrators, High and Low should be set only by someone who knows both routers and the topology. One exception is that a router with no Internet connection, or one behind a firewall that blocks general traffic, should advertise a Low default router preference. The RFC's example is a home user with a tunnel into a firewalled corporate network. The corporate end advertises itself as a default router with Low preference and advertises a specific route for the corporate site prefix, so corporate traffic goes through the tunnel and everything else goes through the home ISP.

Another example has routers X (best for 2002::/16, a 6to4 gateway) and Y (best for ::/0). Making all three host types work well takes a different advertisement for each: both routers as default routers for type A, router X with High preference for type B, and the ::/0 route at Low preference plus 2002::/16 at Medium on router X for type C. Section 5.2 covers a multi-homed host with an isolated network, where the isolated router advertises a route for its network prefix and either no default router role or a Low preference.
sections.plainLanguage: A router should only hang up a few well-chosen signs, and a person has to decide on them. For example, the door into a locked office should say 'not for general traffic'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A malicious node could send Router Advertisements with High preference or specific routes to pull traffic away from legitimate routers. The RFC notes that such a node could already do the same in other ways, for example by forging advertisements with a zero Router Lifetime from the other routers, and that advertising a specific prefix would only make the attack less noticeable. It concludes there is no significant incremental impact on Internet infrastructure security.

A malicious node could also set an infinite lifetime in a Route Information Option so a route lingers. Unlike a similar attack with Prefix Information Options, this causes router reachability probing to continue indefinitely but does not cause a lack of connectivity. Overloading hosts with many routes or frequent advertisements is possible, as it already is with Prefix Information Options. The RFC points to RFC 3756 for trust models and to work in the SEND working group on securing router discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: A prankster could put up fake signs, but he could already do that before. The memo says this does not make things much worse.

fields.name: Prf
fields.desc: Default Router Preference: 01 High, 00 Medium, 11 Low, 10 reserved.

fields.name: Resvd
fields.desc: Unused. Zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Router Lifetime
fields.desc: If zero, Prf is set to 00 and ignored.

items.label: Low
items.desc: Use this router or route only when better ones are not available.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: MUST NOT be sent. Treated as 00 in the header and the whole option is ignored in a Route Information Option.
